title: Teej and Gangaur: Rajasthani jewellery traditions to wear
description: A guide to Rajasthani jewellery for Teej and Gangaur: what borla, aad, bajuband and haathphool are, and how to wear them with leheriya sarees and poshaks.
intro: Teej and Gangaur are two of Rajasthan's most loved women's festivals, and both are a reason to bring out traditional jewellery: a borla on the forehead, an aad or Kundan necklace, bajuband on the arms and plenty of bangles. You do not need a family heirloom collection to wear the look. Knowing what each piece is and where it sits lets you put together a Rajasthani-style outfit with just a few well-chosen pieces.

sections.heading: The two festivals in brief
paragraphs: Hariyali Teej falls in the monsoon month of Shravan. It is associated with Goddess Parvati and her union with Shiva, and is celebrated by married women and young girls with swings, songs, mehendi and green clothing that echoes the rains. Leheriya, the wave-patterned tie-dye fabric of Rajasthan, is the classic Teej outfit, and many households make ghewar for the day.

Gangaur begins right after Holi and runs for around two and a half weeks in many places. Women worship Gauri (Parvati), often with clay idols of Isar and Gangaur. Married women traditionally pray for their husbands' wellbeing and unmarried girls for a good partner. Processions in cities like Jaipur are famous, and the exact rituals differ between Marwar, Mewar, Shekhawati and other regions.

sections.heading: Rajasthani jewellery pieces and what they are
paragraphs: Names vary between regions and communities, but these are the pieces you will see most often during both festivals.
list: Borla or rakhdi: a round, bead-like ornament worn at the centre of the forehead, hanging from the hair parting. In many Rajasthani communities it is linked with married women.
Aad: a broad, flat necklace that sits close to the neck like a collar, usually set with Kundan or stones and finished with drops.
Timaniya and gulbandh: close-fitting necklaces, sometimes on thread, with stones or gold-tone plaques.
Bajuband: an armlet worn on the upper arm, above the elbow.
Haathphool: a hand ornament connecting a bracelet to one or more rings across the back of the hand.
Nath: a nose ring, often large with a chain to the hair for festive and bridal wear.
Kada, punchi and chooda: bangles and bracelets, with chooda sets especially common for newly married women.
Payal and bichhiya: anklets and toe rings.

sections.heading: Dressing for Teej
paragraphs: Green is the Teej colour for many women, usually in leheriya or bandhej. Gold-tone Kundan with green, red or pink stones looks rich against green fabric. Green glass bangles mixed with a couple of gold-tone kadas are an easy, traditional touch.

Because Teej is about swings, outdoor gatherings and sometimes rain, choose jewellery that moves well. Medium jhumkas instead of very heavy chandbalis, a necklace that will not swing into your face on a jhoola, and anklets that are secure. Keep plated pieces away from wet clothes; if they get damp, dry them with a soft cloth as soon as you can.
If you are wearing a leheriya saree to work or a daytime event, a pair of [Meenakari earrings](/women/earrings) and bangles in the saree colours are often enough.

sections.heading: Dressing for Gangaur
paragraphs: Gangaur falls in spring, and women often wear bright pinks, reds, yellows and oranges. The traditional Rajput poshak, a kurti and kanchli worn with a ghaghra and odhni, is a lovely choice for the main day. It pairs naturally with an aad or wide Kundan necklace, a borla, bajuband and a full set of bangles.

The odhni or dupatta usually covers the head for the puja, so the borla and earrings frame the face from under the fabric. Pick earrings that are long enough to peek out, such as chandbalis or jhumkas on a chain.

sections.heading: Building the look without an heirloom box
paragraphs: Traditional Rajasthani sets can be heavy and expensive to own in full. A practical way to get the look is to choose three anchor pieces: a Kundan necklace close to the neck that does the job of an aad, matching earrings, and a statement forehead piece. Bangles and a bajuband complete it. Our [Kundan necklace sets](/women/necklaces) come with earrings, which covers two of the three.

Jaipur is widely known for Kundan and Meenakari work, so these styles feel especially at home for Rajasthani festivals. Meenakari's bright enamel colours on the reverse or front of a piece suit leheriya and bandhej prints well.

For newlyweds celebrating their first Teej or Gangaur, which many families mark with extra ceremony, a lighter version of the bridal look works nicely. Our [bridal jewellery](/women/bridal-jewellery) page has ideas you can scale down.

faq.q: What is a borla in Rajasthani jewellery?
faq.a: A borla, also called rakhdi, is a round forehead ornament worn at the hair parting. In many Rajasthani communities it is associated with married women.

faq.q: What colour should I wear for Teej?
faq.a: Green is traditional for Hariyali Teej in many families, often in leheriya or bandhej, though bright pinks and reds are also popular.

faq.q: Which jewellery goes with a leheriya saree?
faq.a: Gold-tone Kundan or colourful Meenakari earrings, a medium necklace and green or multicoloured bangles all suit leheriya.

faq.q: What is the difference between aad and a choker?
faq.a: Both sit close to the neck. An aad is a traditional Rajasthani piece that is usually broader and flatter, with drops along the lower edge.
